“The war and related events are creating additional upward pressure on inflation and are weighing on global economic activity.” In the monetary policy literature, such adverse supply shocks shift the inflation–output trade-off: Taylor-rule and inflation-targeting frameworks (as implemented by the Federal Reserve) imply tighter policy to anchor expectations when inflation rises above target, even at the cost of softer growth. Evidence from Romer and Romer’s narrative approach underscores the effectiveness of clear, credible tightening in reducing inflation persistence, while the inflation-at-risk perspective suggests that raising the policy rate and shrinking the balance sheet can lower the upper tail of future inflation outcomes. The FOMC’s concurrent hike to a 3.75–4.00% target range and ongoing QT are therefore consistent with these frameworks, partially offsetting the otherwise negative implications of the war for inflation and activity.
